slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time, the code initializes and exports a video player component that accesses and configures HTML5 video elements using the video.js library and a custom Vue.js wrapper. It reads video source URLs and types (including HLS, FLV, RTMP, MP4) from component properties and sets up playback with appropriate tech handlers, including network streaming via HTTP and RTMP protocols. This enables video playback functionality with network streaming capabilities, but does not perform any suspicious data exfiltration or system execution.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code is a Vue.js component wrapping the video.js player library to provide video playback functionality supporting multiple streaming protocols (HLS, FLV, RTMP, MP4). It initializes video players, sets up event listeners, and manages video playback states. There is no evidence of obfuscation, destructive DOM manipulation, environment-based sabotage, or unauthorized code execution. The code does not perform any suspicious data exfiltration, system command execution, or inclusion of large binary payloads. Compared to the known malicious patterns, it lacks any destructive or covert behavior such as blanking the DOM, embedding large video files for unauthorized distribution, or executing obfuscated local modules. The usage of video.js and Vue.js is standard and consistent with legitimate video player implementations.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (when the web application loads in the browser), the code checks for the presence and value of the VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY environment variable and verifies if the application is running on a hardcoded list of allowed domains in production; if these checks fail, it sets document.body.innerHTML to an empty string, resulting in the entire web page being erased and the application rendered unusable for end users.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs destructive actions by blanking the entire web page if the deployment environment does not meet specific, hardcoded criteria. This is not a standard practice and is indicative of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not contain logic that disables or destroys the application based on deployment environment or domain. Normal frontend code does not erase the UI for users based on environment variables or domain checks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Domain and environment variable checks are sometimes used for licensing enforcement or feature gating, but legitimate implementations do not destroy the user interface or application functionality as a consequence.
key_indicators: Destructive DOM manipulation (document.body.innerHTML = '')
Hardcoded allow-list of domains in frontend code
Conditional logic tied to environment variables (VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY, NODE_ENV)
Sabotage logic triggered only in production environments
Absence of user notification or error handling before destructive action

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when the web application is loaded in the browser)
execution_context.file_location: main JavaScript bundle (code injected by the package, typically in the entry point or a core module)

package_info.why_malicious: The package embeds code that intentionally sabotages web applications by erasing the UI if the app is deployed on domains not present in a hardcoded allow-list. This retaliatory logic is triggered in production environments and is designed to break unauthorized deployments, constituting a form of vigilante or destructive malware.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code is included in the web application via the @jayxuz/vue3-admin-icons npm package during the build process.
attack_chain.leads_to: The malicious logic becomes part of the deployed JavaScript bundle.

attack_chain.action: When the application is loaded in the browser, the injected code executes and checks the deployment environment, including environment variables and the current domain.
attack_chain.leads_to: The code determines if the application is running on an unauthorized domain in a production environment.

attack_chain.action: If the domain is not on the hardcoded allow-list and NODE_ENV is 'production', the code erases the web page content by setting document.body.innerHTML to an empty string.
attack_chain.leads_to: The application UI is destroyed, making the web app unusable for end users on unauthorized domains.

behavioral_signatures: Frontend JavaScript code that checks document.domain against a hardcoded allow-list
Destructive DOM manipulation such as setting document.body.innerHTML to an empty string
Conditional sabotage logic based on environment variables (e.g., VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY, NODE_ENV)
Sabotage actions triggered only in production environments
file_indicators: JavaScript files containing checks for document.domain against specific domains: 'localhost', 'chu1204505056.gitee.io', '127.0.0.1', 'vue-admin-beautiful.com'
References to VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY and NODE_ENV in frontend code
Presence of code that sets document.body.innerHTML = ''
network_indicators: None (the code does not perform any network communication or exfiltration in this snippet)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Automated scanners should analyze JavaScript bundles for hardcoded domain allow-lists combined with destructive DOM actions, such as setting document.body.innerHTML to an empty string. Flag any package or code that erases the UI based on environment variables or production checks. Review for the presence of sabotage logic that disables the application outside of specific domains, especially when tied to environment variables like VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY and NODE_ENV.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At package publish and install time, the package includes large binary .ts files (MPEG-TS video clips) in the published artifact, allowing the download and local storage of video segments, resulting in the ability to reconstruct full movies from the npm registry.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Software packages are expected to contain source code and essential assets, not large video files. The inclusion of multi-gigabyte MPEG-TS video data is a clear abuse of the npm registry, as it serves no software function and is indicative of unauthorized media distribution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages contain code and small assets necessary for the software to function. Here, the package is used solely as a file hosting mechanism for pirated or unauthorized media, with no legitimate software functionality.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages may include small demo videos or images for documentation, but never full-length movies or large media libraries as primary content.
key_indicators: Presence of large .ts (MPEG-TS) files in the package root directory
Each package size (~54.5 MB) far exceeds typical npm package size
No actual executable code or software functionality present in the package
File extensions and binary signatures match MPEG-TS video format, not TypeScript

execution_context.trigger: at package publish and install time
execution_context.file_location: package root directory (multiple .ts files, e.g., video1.ts, video2.ts)

package_info.package_versions: all published versions (since at least Dec 4, 2023)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages abuse the npm registry by storing and distributing large, non-software media files (movies, video clips, and associated metadata), violating the platform's terms of service and potentially facilitating the distribution of pirated content. This undermines the integrity and intended use of the software supply chain by turning the registry into a file hosting service for unauthorized media.

attack_chain.action: Attacker splits a movie into multiple video clips (.ts files) and prepares associated metadata (JSON comments) for each segment.
attack_chain.leads_to: Preparation of package artifacts containing video segments and metadata for upload

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes multiple npm packages (wlwz-*) each containing a segment of the movie and its associated metadata files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Packages containing video and metadata are available for download from the npm registry

attack_chain.action: Users or automated scripts download all related wlwz-* packages to reconstruct the full movie and its metadata locally.
attack_chain.leads_to: Distribution and consumption of pirated media via npm, bypassing intended software supply chain controls

behavioral_signatures: npm packages containing large binary files with .ts extension in the root directory
Packages with no executable code or software functionality present
Packages with large JSON files containing time-synced comments or video metadata
file_indicators: *.ts files in package root (binary MPEG-TS video, not TypeScript source)
comments.json or similar large metadata files in package root
Package size >50MB with no code or minimal code content
network_indicators: No direct network indicators (malware does not exfiltrate data or contact C2 servers), but bulk download activity of wlwz-* packages from npm may indicate abuse
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Flag npm packages that contain large binary files with .ts extensions (excluding TypeScript source files), especially when package size exceeds typical thresholds (e.g., >10MB) and there is no corresponding executable code. Monitor for packages with large JSON metadata files unrelated to software functionality. Automated detection should alert on packages with a high storage-to-code ratio and non-software content. Additionally, monitor for bulk downloads of similarly named packages (e.g., wlwz-*) as this may indicate attempts to reconstruct pirated media.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time or when npm test is run, the code loads and immediately executes the bind() function from the obfuscated play.js file, initiating the malware dropper chain and subsequent malicious actions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly executing an obfuscated local module during import or test is highly atypical and is a common initial entry point for malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not execute obfuscated or side-effectful code automatically on import or during test scripts.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some test scripts may run setup or initialization code, but not obfuscated or hidden logic that triggers further execution chains.
key_indicators: Immediate execution of obfuscated local module on import/test
Non-standard use of test script for code execution
Absence of user interaction or consent

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains heavily obfuscated JavaScript code that functions as both a dropper and a remote access trojan (RAT). It performs environment checks to selectively target systems, downloads and executes additional payloads, and establishes a persistent, unauthenticated HTTP server for arbitrary remote code execution, all without user knowledge or consent.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code is executed via npm test or import, triggering the bind() function.
Dropper performs environment checks and conditionally executes or downloads further payloads.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware is deployed and/or additional payloads are executed.

attack_chain.action: Persistence is established by launching play-share.js as a detached process.
RAT HTTP server is started, allowing remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistent remote access and control.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of obfuscated JavaScript files during npm install, test, or import
Spawning of detached Node.js background processes running secondary scripts
Creation of local HTTP server on non-standard port (e.g., 3004) for command execution
Environment checks targeting Windows and active user environments before payload execution
Conditional download and execution of remote payloads based on hidden configuration
file_indicators: Batch files with random names in temporary directories
network_indicators: HTTP server listening on port 3004 for incoming command requests
Outbound HTTP GET requests to attacker-controlled URLs for payload download
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of obfuscated JavaScript files during npm install, test, or import. Flag packages that spawn detached Node.js processes or create local HTTP servers on non-standard ports such as 3004. Detect creation of suspicious files including node.compress.exe, node.compress.lock.log, and batch files with random names in temp directories. Watch for outbound HTTP requests to unknown or suspicious domains and for local servers listening for command parameters. Use static analysis to identify high-entropy, obfuscated code and dynamic analysis to observe process spawning, file creation, and network activity indicative of RAT behavior.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code defines the module as an ES module and exports a null default value, resulting in no data processing or side effects.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is not inherently malicious, but the presence of a package with a single-character name and no functional code is highly unusual. Such packages are often created unintentionally due to typographical errors and can be abused in the future if the code is updated to include malicious payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages typically provide useful functionality or utilities, whereas this package exports only a null value and performs no operations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Test, placeholder, or namespace-reserving packages may sometimes be published with minimal or no functionality, but these are usually clearly marked or not widely downloaded.
key_indicators: Single-character package name ('-')
index.js exports only null as default
No functional code or logic present
Unusually high download count for a non-functional package

package_info.why_malicious: The package '-' is not currently malicious, but its existence and high download count are due to accidental installations caused by typographical errors in npm commands. Its presence in projects is unintentional and could be abused in the future if the package contents change to include malicious code. The risk is that such packages can be silently included in builds, creating a potential supply chain attack vector by providing an opportunity for attackers to later introduce malicious payloads into a widely distributed, trusted dependency.

attack_chain.action: Accidental installation of the '-' package due to typographical errors in npm commands or package.json dependencies.
attack_chain.leads_to: The package is included in the project, potentially as a placeholder for future malicious code, creating a supply chain risk if the package contents are updated with malicious payloads.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of single-character or command-like package names in dependencies (e.g., '-', 'i', 'g', 'D')
Packages with no functional code or only skeleton code (e.g., exporting null or empty modules)
High download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation
file_indicators: package.json dependencies including '-', 'i', 'g', 'D', or other single-character/command-like names
index.js file that only exports null or an empty module
package.json scripts section with non-functional or placeholder scripts referencing missing files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan package.json and package-lock.json for dependencies with suspicious names such as '-', 'i', 'g', or names matching npm command flags. Flag packages that have no functional code or only export null/empty modules in their main files. Check for non-functional npm scripts referencing missing files. Monitor for sudden inclusion of such packages in projects, especially if not explicitly added by developers, and alert on high download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation.

matched_knowledge.source_package: Trojanized jQuery (multiple packages, e.g., icnes, stylesyosx, imagegs, etc.) (npm (also distributed via GitHub and jsDelivr CDN))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when the script is loaded, the code injects external scripts into the page, including a deprecated version of Ionicons and a remote script (slim.js) hosted on jsDelivr, which itself contains the trojanized jQuery. This enables the delivery and execution of further malicious payloads and establishes persistence for the attack.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Injecting remote scripts from untrusted or attacker-controlled sources is a common technique for loading additional malware. The use of misleading deprecation warnings and outdated libraries is intended to trick users or developers into trusting the injected content.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal icon libraries do not inject unrelated remote scripts or force the use of outdated versions without user consent. They also do not load scripts from untrusted CDNs or chain to further malicious payloads.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script injection is sometimes used by legitimate plugin loaders, but not in core icon libraries and never with misleading warnings or by loading unrelated, potentially malicious scripts.
key_indicators: Dynamic injection of remote scripts from attacker-controlled or untrusted CDNs
Use of misleading deprecation warnings to mask malicious activity
Loading of outdated or unrelated library versions
Chaining to further malicious payloads (e.g., slim.js containing trojanized jQuery)
Script injection occurring outside of user-initiated actions

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when icons.js or min.js is loaded and executed in the browser (typically during page load or dynamic script injection).
execution_context.file_location: icons.js, min.js (in package root or distributed via CDN)

package_info.package_name: Trojanized jQuery (multiple packages, e.g., icnes, stylesyosx, imagegs, etc.)
package_info.package_manager: npm (also distributed via GitHub and jsDelivr CDN)
package_info.package_versions: Multiple (see list, e.g., icnes@8.0.0, stylesyosx@9.0.3, etc.)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages contain a trojanized version of jQuery in which the 'end' prototype function is maliciously modified to exfiltrate all form data from the page to attacker-controlled domains whenever it is called, either directly or indirectly (such as via fadeTo). The packages are distributed under misleading names, often include personal files unrelated to the package's purpose, and use unique exfiltration URLs to evade detection. This enables large-scale theft of sensitive user input (credentials, PII, etc.) from any site using the compromised packages.

attack_chain.action: User installs or includes a malicious package (via npm, GitHub, or CDN).
attack_chain.leads_to: Trojanized jQuery or loader script is present in the application.

attack_chain.action: Malicious jQuery file (or loader script) is loaded and executed in the browser, often via dynamic script injection.
attack_chain.leads_to: Trojanized jQuery is present in the page context, ready to intercept user actions.

attack_chain.action: User or application code calls jQuery's end or fadeTo function (directly or indirectly), triggering the malicious code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious end function is executed, capturing form data.

attack_chain.action: All form data on the page is serialized, hex-encoded, and exfiltrated via a GET request to an attacker-controlled domain.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives sensitive user input (credentials, PII, etc.) from the compromised site.

behavioral_signatures: Modification of jQuery prototype methods (especially end) to include network requests or data exfiltration logic
Unexpected network requests triggered by UI actions (such as fadeTo animation or end function calls)
Hex-encoded form data sent to external or suspicious domains
Dynamic injection of remote scripts from untrusted or attacker-controlled sources (e.g., via document.createElement in icon libraries)
Presence of misleading deprecation warnings in icon or utility scripts
file_indicators: jquery.min.js, all-min.js, slim.js, registration.min.js, icon.min.js, fontawesome.js (with modified end function or added network logic)
Presence of personal files (e.g., npm cache, npm logs, termux.properties) in the package root directory
icons.js, min.js files that inject remote scripts or reference external CDNs
network_indicators: Requests to jsdelivr.net/gh/indexsc/libs/slim.js or similar GitHub-backed CDN URLs
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan JavaScript dependencies for unauthorized modifications to core library prototype methods, especially jQuery's end. Use static analysis to compare jQuery source code against known-good versions and flag any added network or data exfiltration logic. Monitor for unexpected network requests containing serialized or hex-encoded form data sent to suspicious or attacker-controlled domains. Flag packages that include personal files or inject remote scripts from untrusted sources. Analyze icon and utility scripts for dynamic script injection and misleading deprecation warnings. Combine static and dynamic analysis to detect both code modifications and runtime exfiltration behaviors.
